name: Sir Chris Hoy Gold Post Box (Hanover Street)
description: This pillar box at the foot of Hanover Street, on the corner with Princes Street, is the second of Edinburgh's two gold post boxes honouring Sir Chris Hoy. Royal Mail painted it gold in August 2012 to mark his gold medal in the men's team sprint, won alongside Philip Hindes and Jason Kenny - a different medal from the keirin gold that earned the city's other gold box in Hunter Square. A hometown collecting two gold boxes was unusual under the nationwide scheme, since most gold medallists only ever earned their city one; Hoy's second gold in the same Games meant Edinburgh became one of the few places with a pair.
interesting_fact: The team sprint final was itself a piece of Olympic drama: Hindes crashed on the opening lap of the first-round heat, triggering a restart under a rule permitting a rerun after any first-lap fall - a decision some observers suspected was tactical, though officials ruled it accidental. On the restart, Hoy, Hindes and Kenny broke their own qualifying world record, stopping the clock at 42.600 seconds. This box sits a short walk from the New Town streets where Hoy grew up before his track career began at Meadowbank Velodrome, just a few miles east.

name: Harvey Nichols Edinburgh
description: Harvey Nichols opened on the east side of St Andrew Square in 2002, built to designs by Edinburgh-based CDA Architects - the same practice behind the neighbouring Multrees Walk development and Edinburgh Bus Station. At five storeys and around 100,000 square feet, it was, at the time of opening, the largest Harvey Nichols store outside London, part of a wave of investment that transformed this corner of the New Town from a quiet Georgian square into the city's most upscale shopping quarter. Multrees Walk, the pedestrian street of luxury boutiques linking the square to the older St James Centre, followed the year after in 2003.
interesting_fact: The top floor houses the Forth Floor restaurant and bar, whose external terrace looks north over the Firth of Forth - the estuary the store is named after, sharing its view with the much older Melville Monument obelisk standing at the square's centre. St Andrew Square itself dates to the 1760s, the very first phase of James Craig's New Town plan, and was originally Edinburgh's most fashionable residential address; its early residents included the philosopher David Hume, whose townhouse there predates Harvey Nichols' glass-and-stone facade by well over two centuries.

name: Milnes Bar
description: Milnes Bar opened at 35 Hanover Street in 1910 as a spirit merchants' shop before growing into a full public house by the 1950s. It was during those same decades that it earned its enduring nickname, the "Poets' Pub" - the gathering place at the centre of the Scottish Literary Renaissance, drawing figures including Hugh MacDiarmid, Sorley MacLean and Norman MacCaig. MacDiarmid, whose 1926 poem A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle helped launch that revival in Scots-language verse, called Milnes his favourite howff, and the bar was redecorated in his memory in 1985 with photographs and a painted sign marking the connection.
interesting_fact: The bar's basement snug was nicknamed the "Little Kremlin" by its regulars, only half-jokingly, for the intensity of the political arguments and poetic manifestos traded there. MacDiarmid's own Milnes-fuelled reputation later found its way into fiction: Alasdair Gray's 1984 novel 1982, Janine draws directly on his legendary sessions at the bar. A century on from its 1910 opening, Milnes still trades as a pub barely a hundred metres from where its two gold-painted Chris Hoy post boxes sit on the same street.
